li.a: Australian Dictionary of Biography: Darcy Ezekiel Dugan
The Glebe Society: Darcy Ezekiel Dugan (1920-1991)
The Glebe Society: Darcy Dugan, memoirs and reader recollections
City of Parramatta History and Heritage: Australia's Most Notorious Escape Artist, Darcy Dugan
Sydney Morning Herald: Larrikin thief's last gamble marks his grave

content.p: Darcy Ezekiel Dugan was an armed robber who became better known for the prisons he got out of than for the crimes that put him in them. Over four decades he escaped from custody in New South Wales again and again: from a prison van, from a cell in the middle of Sydney's court complex, and, most famously, through the roof of a moving prison tram. The press called him "Houdini". The Glebe Society counts six successful escapes and four failed attempts, and says that to Dugan, the prison system's job was to keep him in and his job was to get out.

His story has a darker side. In 1950 a judge sentenced him to death after a bank hold-up in which his partner shot and seriously injured the bank manager. The sentence was commuted, and he was sent to Grafton Jail, a prison where, the dictionary says, men thought beyond reform were treated brutally. Years afterwards his evidence about it helped change how New South Wales treated prisoners. He died in 1991, and his memoir came out twenty-one years later.

Dugan was born on 29 August 1920 in Newtown, in Sydney's inner west. The Australian Dictionary of Biography says his father, Ezekiel, was a mason; the Glebe Society calls him an ornamental tiler and a former bare-knuckle boxing champion. The family was Irish Catholic, and Darcy went to school with the Christian Brothers. The Glebe Society says that his parents married in 1933 and divorced five years later, and that he stayed with his father.

By his early teens he was shoplifting around Annandale with schoolmates, among them Lenny McPherson, who later became a notorious figure in Sydney's underworld. According to the Glebe Society he sold stolen cosmetics to cinema usherettes and to the brothel-keeper Tilly Devine. The Australian Dictionary of Biography describes him as a juvenile cat burglar with a fascination for locks.

After his tenth appearance in the Children's Court, Dugan was sent in 1937 to the Gosford Training School for Boys, found guilty of stealing from his uncle's hotel according to the dictionary. The dictionary says he met brutal treatment there from guards and other boys. He ran away, and the pattern that followed, in the dictionary's words, was crime, capture, bashing, gaol and escape. Before he turned twenty-one he had been held at Long Bay, Emu Plains Prison Farm, Goulburn Reformatory and Oberon Prison Farm.

In June 1942 he joined the Citizen Military Forces for full-time service and was posted to Cowra for sapper training. On 22 July he left without permission. While on the run he committed a burglary, and in October the Sydney Quarter Sessions gave him two years. He was discharged from the army that day. Between sentences he taught ballroom dancing in Sydney studios, and the Glebe Society says he also won money in competitive dancing.

In January 1946 Dugan and Harry Mitchell, both held over a burglary, were being driven from Long Bay to a court at Burwood in a prison van. The Glebe Society says Dugan used a screwdriver made from a prison fork to loosen a ventilator panel in the roof, and both men squeezed out. They were caught, but within days of his recapture, in March, Dugan was loose again.

On 4 March 1946 he was being carried between Darlinghurst Courthouse and Long Bay on a prison tram. As it passed the Sydney Cricket Ground, he cut a hole in the roof with a kitchen knife and got out. The Australian Dictionary of Biography says he escaped with another prisoner near Centennial Park and was caught a day later. According to the Glebe Society, the newspapers called the escape "sensational" and "daring" and called him "the India-rubber man". He had nothing to eat or drink, and surrendered at Boronia Park after 37 hours of freedom. The City of Parramatta notes that the tram survives at the Sydney Tramway Museum.

He was sentenced to three and a half years in Bathurst. When he was released in 1949 he legally became Darcy Clare by deed poll, took a warehouse job and began saving for a truck. The Glebe Society says he lost a job at a canned butter factory when police told his employer who he was.

In August 1949 Dugan was in the dock with William Cecil Mears after a failed armed robbery. The Glebe Society says that within half an hour of reaching Long Bay the pair had got through a lock, part of a roof and two walls, then boarded a city tram. The Australian Dictionary of Biography says they were free for little more than a week. A reward of 500 pounds was offered, and they were found in a hide-out at Lugarno, according to the Glebe Society. Judge Adrian Curlewis gave each a ten-year sentence.

In December the two were in the Central Court of Petty Sessions. Mears had Dugan called as a witness in another matter. During the lunch recess he sawed through the cell bars with a hacksaw blade, which the Glebe Society says he had carried threaded between his shoulder blades. The dictionary says he is alleged to have written "Gone to Gowings", a popular advertising slogan, on the wall. The two went down a drainpipe and into the Christmas shoppers. Rumours spread that they were disguised as women, as Santa Claus or as hospital patients.

On 13 January 1950 they robbed the Ultimo branch of the Commonwealth Bank. Mears shot and seriously injured the manager, Leslie Nalder. Sources differ on the second person hurt: the Sydney Morning Herald and the Pyrmont History Group say a customer, the Glebe Society a clerk. The Pyrmont History Group adds that the tellers were armed, and that the robbers drove to Glebe and switched to a second car. The Glebe Society says they left the getaway car outside a house in Eglinton Road and were picked up by Lennie McPherson. Police found their hideout at Collaroy in February, after an informant, according to the Glebe Society, and Detective Sergeant Ray Kelly arrested both men. It was the first of four arrests of Dugan by Kelly.

At Central Court in May 1950 Dugan tried to escape again. The Glebe Society says he had made a key from a belt buckle, using a mould of a handcuff lock, and had undone his handcuffs, but a bolted door stopped him. In June Justice Leslie Herron sentenced both men to death; the Sydney Morning Herald says the charge was wounding with intent to murder. The Labor government of the McGirr, narrowly returned in that month's election, commuted both sentences to life in December.

The two were sent to Grafton, the toughest prison in the state, which prisoners called the Bloodhouse. The dictionary says it ran a harsh regime for men thought unlikely ever to reform. Dugan twice tried to get out and took part in a failed mass break-out. The Glebe Society says that in 1953 he organised a breakout of about a dozen prisoners who bolted after a chapel service, and that at one stage he pretended to be insane, refusing food and water until he was, in its words, as thin as a match. He was force-fed at Long Bay and returned to Grafton.

In 1953 a petition signed by two hundred people, among them the Anglican Bishop of Canberra and Goulburn, Ernest Burgmann, asked the governor to release him and two other men from solitary confinement. A second petition from five thousand Grafton residents asked for an end to the system used for intractable prisoners. Neither succeeded, the dictionary says.

He was moved to Parramatta in 1956 and tried to escape again in 1958, after which he went back to Grafton. The Glebe Society says that at Parramatta in 1957 a fellow prisoner, George Freeman, told him that McPherson was a police informant who had betrayed him. After that Dugan studied Houdini and practised swallowing and bringing up cutlery. Through the 1960s he was moved between Long Bay, Grafton, Parramatta, a forestry camp and Bathurst. In 1960 the state attorney-general, Reg Downing, recommended that his release be considered in 1964 if he behaved, and the minister of justice, Jack Mannix, later repeated the advice.

He left Bathurst on licence in September 1967. The Glebe Society says he sold his story to a newspaper, worked at Ted Noffs' Wayside Chapel in Kings Cross, wrote a play and acted in a 1969 production of Fortune and Men's Eyes, a play set in a prison. He also campaigned against police corruption and violence in the prisons. In 1969 he was arrested over a jewellery shop robbery and in May 1970 sentenced to fourteen years. The Glebe Society says he claimed he was innocent; the City of Parramatta says corrupt police framed him for a crime he did not commit. The dictionary records the arrest and sentence without comment on guilt.

From prison he gave evidence to the royal commission into New South Wales prisons in 1977 and 1978. The dictionary says it led to significant changes in how inmates were treated. The City of Parramatta says he described daily beatings and even boiling water thrown on prisoners at Grafton, and that Bob Campbell wrote a song from his testimony. Separately, Dugan sued Mirror Newspapers for defamation, and in December 1978 lost an appeal in the High Court because he was a prisoner at the time of the alleged defamation.

Dugan was released in May 1980 and, on 12 July, married Janice Simmonds at the Wayside Chapel. She was the sister of another escaper, Kevin Simmonds, and the couple lived in Canberra before splitting but stayed friends. In July 1981 he was arrested over an attempted armed robbery, which the Glebe Society places at a service station in Glebe. He was released in November 1985.
content.h2: The last years and the memoir
content.p: After 1985 Dugan lived at Glebe House, a halfway house, and the Glebe Society says he developed Parkinson's disease there. The dictionary mentions a stroke in 1985. Sources disagree about where he died on 22 August 1991: the dictionary and the Glebe Society say Cabramatta, the Glebe Society specifying a nursing home, while the Pyrmont History Group and the City of Parramatta say Glebe. He was buried at Rookwood Cemetery. A person who did community service at Glebe House in the late 1980s remembered a silent, shrunken old man who kept wandering off, and whom police regarded as a "sort of wayward pet", but that recollection is one reader's memory and not a documented account.

The Pyrmont History Group credits him with a second career as rehabilitator and witness, and says he spent half his long life in gaol. The City of Parramatta puts his time inside at 43 years; the bookseller's summary of his memoir says 44. Bloodhouse was written in his own hand in prison and smuggled out. The Glebe Society says he told the journalist Michael Tatlow not to publish it until he, McPherson, Kelly and Fred Krahe had "turned to dust". Tatlow wrote the closing chapters, and the book appeared in 2012.

Mears, the man beside him in the Ultimo case, served 15 years and was released in 1965, the Sydney Morning Herald reported. He died in 2002 at 82, living alone in a Waterloo housing flat. A lottery ticket found among his things paid for his headstone.
